p.t: In short
Do not set a price from **follower count** alone. Look at the whole package.
Check the **engagement rate** first: the share of followers who like, comment or share. It often matters more than size.

Write down **who may use the content, and how**, before you pay.
**Test with smaller creators** before you commit a large budget.
Pay more for **exclusive or paid-ad use** than for a single organic post.
Pricing, budgeting and negotiation
Fee drivers
An **influencer** (a person with an online audience who promotes products) is paid according to several factors.
The **follower count** (how many people follow the account) alone does not set the fee.
A larger audience usually commands a higher price, but that link is not reliable, so audience size must be weighed against the other factors.
The **engagement rate** (the share of followers who like, comment or share) often matters more than follower count.
Example: an account with about 500,000 followers and a 20% engagement rate can ask for more than an account with 1 million followers and a 5-6% engagement rate, because its audience is more active
and more likely to buy. Engagement rate is a strong signal of what a creator can charge.
**Price the whole package**, not audience size alone.

Niche fit (how closely the creator's narrow topic area matches your product), content quality, engagement rate and the campaign's brand objective (the goal you want your brand to reach through a planned
marketing push, called a campaign) together determine what is fair and justified.
For **UGC** (user-generated content: videos made by creators for a brand) that the creator posts on their own account, follower count and engagement rate significantly raise the price.
The engagement rate on the creator's Instagram or TikTok account should be above **4-5%**. If the brand only uses the video itself, follower count and engagement matter little.
Creators who serve a narrow niche or are true specialists charge more, because few creators cover that niche
and the market is less saturated (less crowded with competitors). Confirm that the creator's niche and expertise level match what you are budgeting for.
Influencers who are **one of only a few** covering a specific task usually charge more. True specialists in their domain charge even higher rates.
Content quality and track record
Content quality can justify a higher fee.
Relevant factors are production value (how polished the filming and editing are), brand alignment (how well the creator fits your brand), how long the creator has worked as an influencer,
how much content they have produced, and how well they produce it.
A creator with a **proven track record** (a history of good results), high engagement and a recognised name in the industry, who works in content full time, will usually ask for a higher fee.
Leaders in their niche, such as a well-known tech creator, can command a premium because their expertise adds to the collaboration's success.
A fair fee is a judgment across audience size, engagement, niche expertise, content quality and the brand's goal. Weigh all of these before deciding what is justified.
Define the **usage term** (the rules for how you may use the content) clearly.
State the exclusivity (only your brand may use it) and the usage rights (permission to use the content) you need.
Exclusive use, or the right to repurpose (reuse for another purpose) content across channels and ads, raises the fee.

Price **exclusive usage rights**, and the right to reuse content in paid ads (ads you pay to show) or across several channels, **separately**. Charge a higher fee than for organic use (unpaid posts) on one channel.

Write the granted rights into the contract.
**Document** in writing which rights are granted to whom.

**Royalty** (a share of the money earned instead of a flat price) alternative: a content creator who makes ad material for a brand can be paid about **3%** of the revenue the creative generates in paid ads,
instead of a flat fee. This works only when the brand can attribute (link sales to a source) ad revenue to that content.
Deliverables and campaign complexity
Define **deliverables** (the exact work the creator must hand in) in detail: the exact scope of posts,
stories (temporary posts that vanish after a short time), costs and creative work the creator must deliver. Each additional element raises the compensation.
Assess **campaign complexity** when pricing. Low-effort campaigns leave room to negotiate a lower fee.
Campaigns that need photographers, videographers or specific locations justify higher compensation.
Price UGC by **use case** (what the content will be used for). Videos for paid ads need higher production quality and justify a higher budget.
Organic TikTok content can use lower production quality if it is engaging and attention-grabbing.
The **platform** (the app or site where content is posted) or company used to source the creator (where you find and hire them) is a major price factor, alongside the use case
and the creator's reach (how many people see their posts).
1. **Define the usage term** clearly: state the exclusivity and the usage rights you need for the content.
Exclusive use or the right to repurpose content across channels and ads will raise the fee.
2. **Negotiate** the terms openly with the influencer so both sides are satisfied, and document in writing which rights are granted to whom.
3. Assess the campaign's complexity: low-effort work leaves room to negotiate the price, while high effort such as photographers, videographers or specific locations requires higher compensation.
4. Define the **deliverables** precisely (posts, stories, creative work). Each additional element should increase the compensation.
5. Evaluate the track record: well-known leaders in their niche who make their living from this work charge more, because their expertise contributes to the success of the collaboration.
6. **Negotiate** the final compensation with all of these points factored in, and check that the price fits your budget.
Market benchmarks
Influencers charge anywhere from about **$50 to about $1 million** per collaboration.
Before reaching out, determine where your budget sits within that range.

Know the **market benchmarks** (typical prices to compare against) for audience size, engagement rate, content quality and your niche before negotiating. Without them you risk overpaying or underpaying.
Adjust the market rate for campaign-specific factors such as the influencer's expertise, the complexity of the work and any exclusive rights. Reflect these adjustments in the contract.
Sources disagree on the rates for small creators. Each row below states the condition under which that figure applies.
p.h: Reported rates by creator size and platform

p.t:
Rates depend on reach, engagement, recent performance, platform and whether the creator is paid in cash or in product.
**Celebrity-level creator**

Platform: Any
Reported rate: Can reach about $500,000 per post
When it applies: Large reach; small creators with real engagement deliver similar reach for much less

**Personal trainer, 300,000 followers, more than 10,000 likes and hundreds of comments per post**
Platform: Instagram
Reported rate: $100 per post

When it applies: Real, high engagement relative to follower count
**About 100,000 followers in a niche**
Platform: Instagram

Reported rate: About $5,000
When it applies: Niche creator at this audience size
**Smaller Instagram creators**
Platform: Instagram

Reported rate: Free merchandise, or about $50-$300
When it applies: Smaller audience, lower engagement
**Micro-influencer**

Platform: Any
Reported rate: $50-$100 per influencer
When it applies: Tight budget; with $100-$200 you can hire 2 micro-influencers as an alternative to Meta (the company behind Facebook and Instagram) or TikTok ads

**Many creators still building an audience**
Platform: Any
Reported rate: Free product, or about $100 per post
Reported rates by creator size and platform (continued)

When it applies: Early-stage creators as a low-cost source of photos and video
**100,000-500,000 followers**
Platform: Any
Reported rate: Often an upfront payment (money paid before the work) of about $50-$100, depending on reach

When it applies: Upfront payment may be needed at this size
**Smaller creators**
Platform: Any

Reported rate: Free product in exchange for a review
When it applies: Sometimes the only payment needed for small creators
**TikTok creator**

Platform: TikTok
Reported rate: About $50-$200 per post, depending on reach

When it applies: Creators whose recent posts performed well often charge less
**TikTok creator, about 50,000 followers**
Platform: TikTok

Reported rate: At least $200 for a paid collaboration
When it applies: Paid collaboration at this size
**TikTok creator, about 10,000 followers**

Platform: TikTok
Reported rate: About $100-$200
When it applies: Creator may accept this range

**Reported TikTok price range**
Platform: TikTok
Reported rate: 20 to 45

When it applies: Unit (currency or per-thousand-views basis) is not stated; verify before use
**New freelance UGC creator**

Platform: Fiverr (a website where freelancers sell their services)
Reported rate: Lower prices
When it applies: While still building the review record; suitable for small test budgets
**Platform changes the price.** Instagram creators with a similar follower count often ask for more than TikTok creators.
Compare offers per platform before budgeting, and plan a higher rate for Instagram than for TikTok.
Budget sizing (continued)
Budget sizing
1. Assess the overall marketing budget and set a **reasonable portion** for influencer marketing without compromising the strategy or the business.
2. Prioritise influencers within that budget. If an influencer is out of reach, choose another who fits both budget and goals.
3. Research industry standards for audience size, engagement rate, content quality and your niche so you know the usual rates.
4. Adjust the market rate for expertise, campaign complexity and exclusivity, and reflect this in the contract.
5. Communicate openly about the budget and any constraints during negotiation.
6. Show flexibility through **long-term collaboration**, mutual promotion (both sides promote each other) or affiliate options (the creator earns a commission on each sale they bring).
7. Emphasise the mutual benefit, especially the unique value your brand brings to the influencer's audience.
8. Discuss a **long-term partnership**, in which the rate can be lowered for an extended period.
The influencer budget should be only a **reasonable portion** of the total marketing budget.
Size it so that it does not compromise the overall marketing strategy or the business.
**Never** choose an influencer whose price is outside your budget, even if you strongly want them. Look for an influencer who fits both your budget and your campaign goals.
**Test with smaller creators** before committing large budgets. A high fee for a large influencer can return far less than expected: one reported $15,000 post returned about $2,000 in sales.
Flat versus performance pay
**Flat fee:** pays a fixed amount per deliverable.
Use it when the deliverables and usage rights are fixed in advance and the brand cannot attribute sales to the content.
**Royalty:** about **3%** of the revenue the creative generates in paid ads. Use it only when the brand can attribute ad revenue to that content.
**Small fixed payment plus affiliate commission** (a share of each sale the creator brings): works when the budget is limited.
The creator earns a base amount for the post and more for each sale, which aligns their incentive with yours.
**Affiliate commission** for micro-influencers: the offered range is **6-7%**.
Worked example: a kayak seller offers a local kayaker with a blog or Instagram account 3-5 free kayaks plus a 6% affiliate commission per referral (a sale the creator sends you).
The creator profits from promoting to their niche audience without large upfront costs.

**Flat rate for all creators:** if a brand pays one flat rate to all creators, for example $500 per creator, state in the brief (the written task instructions) or negotiation that there is **no room to negotiate**.
**Story placements** (a spot in the temporary stories section) are usually much cheaper than feed posts for the same creator.
For accounts with roughly 30,000-50,000 followers, a story post is often the better buy for predictable reach.
Story posts give **predictable reach** near the creator's average story views. A feed post (a permanent post on the main profile) or TikTok post can go viral but depends on video quality.
Choose story posts when consistency matters. Choose feed posts when you want **high variance** (results that swing a lot, up or down). You can also negotiate both.
Creators charge more during the **fourth quarter** (October to December) and around holidays. Negotiate and book posts before the season.
Negotiation tactics (continued)
Negotiation tactics
Start with a **low offer** and increase only if the creator pushes back.
Creators who work with you once often accept lower rates the next time.
Open communication about your budget and any constraints often leads influencers to come down in price, especially when they want to work with the brand.
Negotiate the terms openly so that both sides are satisfied.

**Ask for the creator's rate directly.** For a paid Instagram post, contact the account by direct message (a private message) and ask for the creator's rate for a post that gives your store a shout-out (a

public mention).
For industry event sponsorships (paying to be featured at a trade event), **ask for the costs first**, because some are expensive and others are affordable.
**Non-cash offers** (value that is not money), such as long-term collaboration, mutual promotion or affiliate marketing, show flexibility
interviews featuring their expertise.
If your brand gives the influencer's audience **unique value**, the influencer may be more willing to work with you and adjust their rates.
Emphasise this mutual benefit in the negotiation.
**Long-term partnerships** lower the cost per collaboration. Influencers value regular income, and the brand gains a reliable partner who keeps working with them over time.
